revision.text:
<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q1107129]] Wikidata name: sōja [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:39, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}
{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole [[:en:Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>
Whenever a new [[:en:Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>
The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[:en:Inaba|Inaba]]. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>
The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[:en:Sōja|Sōja]] in [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]].
Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q1107129]] Wikidata name: sōja [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:39, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}
{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole [[:en:Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>
Whenever a new [[:en:Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>
The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[:en:Inaba|Inaba]]. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>
The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[:en:Sōja|Sōja]] in [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]].
Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q1107129]] Wikidata name: sōja [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:39, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}
{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole [[:en:Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>
Whenever a new [[:en:Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>
The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[:en:Inaba|Inaba]]. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>
The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[:en:Sōja|Sōja]] in [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]].
Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q1107129]] Wikidata name: sōja [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:39, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}
{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole [[:en:Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>
Whenever a new [[:en:Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>
The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[:en:Inaba|Inaba]]. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>
The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[:en:Sōja|Sōja]] in [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]].
Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q1107129]] Wikidata name: sōja [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:39, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}
{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole [[:en:Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>
Whenever a new [[:en:Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>
The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[:en:Inaba|Inaba]]. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>
The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[:en:Sōja|Sōja]] in [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]].
Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q1107129]] Wikidata name: sōja [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:39, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}
{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole [[:en:Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>
Whenever a new [[:en:Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>
The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[:en:Inaba|Inaba]]. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>
The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[:en:Sōja|Sōja]] in [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]].
Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q1107129]] Wikidata name: sōja [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:39, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}
{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole [[:en:Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>
Whenever a new [[:en:Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>
The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[:en:Inaba|Inaba]]. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>
The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[:en:Sōja|Sōja]] in [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]].
Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q1107129]] Wikidata name: sōja [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:39, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}
{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole [[:en:Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>
Whenever a new [[:en:Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>
The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[:en:Inaba|Inaba]]. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>
The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[:en:Sōja|Sōja]] in [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]].
Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q1107129]] Wikidata name: sōja [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:39, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}
{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole [[:en:Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>
Whenever a new [[:en:Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>
The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[:en:Inaba|Inaba]]. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>
The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[:en:Sōja|Sōja]] in [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]].
Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q1107129]] Wikidata name: sōja [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:39, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}
{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole [[:en:Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>
Whenever a new [[:en:Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>
The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[:en:Inaba|Inaba]]. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>
The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[:en:Sōja|Sōja]] in [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]].
Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q1107129]] Wikidata name: sōja [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:39, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}
{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole [[:en:Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>
Whenever a new [[:en:Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>
The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[:en:Inaba|Inaba]]. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>
The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[:en:Sōja|Sōja]] in [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]].
Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q1107129]] Wikidata name: sōja [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:39, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}
{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole [[:en:Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>
Whenever a new [[:en:Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>
The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[:en:Inaba|Inaba]]. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>
The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[:en:Sōja|Sōja]] in [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]].
Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q1107129]] Wikidata name: sōja [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:39, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}
{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole [[:en:Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>
Whenever a new [[:en:Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>
The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[:en:Inaba|Inaba]]. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>
The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[:en:Sōja|Sōja]] in [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]].
Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q1107129]] Wikidata name: sōja [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:39, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}
{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole [[:en:Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>
Whenever a new [[:en:Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>
The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[:en:Inaba|Inaba]]. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>
The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[:en:Sōja|Sōja]] in [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]].
Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q1107129]] Wikidata name: sōja [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:39, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}
{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole [[:en:Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>
Whenever a new [[:en:Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>
The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[:en:Inaba|Inaba]]. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>
The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[:en:Sōja|Sōja]] in [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]].
Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q1107129]] Wikidata name: sōja [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:39, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}
{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole [[:en:Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>
Whenever a new [[:en:Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>
The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[:en:Inaba|Inaba]]. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>
The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[:en:Sōja|Sōja]] in [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]].
Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q1107129]] Wikidata name: sōja [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:39, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}
{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole [[:en:Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>
Whenever a new [[:en:Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>
The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[:en:Inaba|Inaba]]. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>
The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[:en:Sōja|Sōja]] in [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]].
Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q1107129]] Wikidata name: sōja [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:39, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}
{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole [[:en:Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>
Whenever a new [[:en:Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>
The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[:en:Inaba|Inaba]]. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>
The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[:en:Sōja|Sōja]] in [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]].
Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[da:d:Q1107129]] Wikidata name: sōja [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:39, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}
{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole [[:en:Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>
Whenever a new [[:en:Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>
The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[:en:Inaba|Inaba]]. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>
The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[:en:Sōja|Sōja]] in [[:en:Okayama Prefecture|Okayama Prefecture]].
Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

Wikidata name: sōja
[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:39, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}}
{{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}

{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole {{ill|Provinces of Japan|en|Provinces of Japan|WD=Q860290|lt=province}}. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara period}} under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>

Whenever a new {{ill|Kokushi (official)|en|Kokushi (official)|WD=Q1351234|lt=kokushi}} was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>

The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}, in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of {{ill|Inaba|en|Inaba|WD=Q79501645|lt=Inaba}}. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>

The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of {{ill|Sōja|en|Sōja|WD=Q873536|lt=Sōja}} in {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|en|Okayama Prefecture|WD=Q132936|lt=Okayama Prefecture}}.

Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

Wikidata name: sōja
[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:39, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}}
{{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}

{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole {{ill|Provinces of Japan|en|Provinces of Japan|WD=Q860290|lt=province}}. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara period}} under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>

Whenever a new {{ill|Kokushi (official)|en|Kokushi (official)|WD=Q1351234|lt=kokushi}} was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>

The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}, in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of {{ill|Inaba|en|Inaba|WD=Q79501645|lt=Inaba}}. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>

The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of {{ill|Sōja|en|Sōja|WD=Q873536|lt=Sōja}} in {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|en|Okayama Prefecture|WD=Q132936|lt=Okayama Prefecture}}.

Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

Wikidata name: sōja
[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:39, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}}
{{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}

{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole {{ill|Provinces of Japan|en|Provinces of Japan|WD=Q860290|lt=province}}. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara period}} under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>

Whenever a new {{ill|Kokushi (official)|en|Kokushi (official)|WD=Q1351234|lt=kokushi}} was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>

The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}, in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of {{ill|Inaba|en|Inaba|WD=Q79501645|lt=Inaba}}. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>

The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of {{ill|Sōja|en|Sōja|WD=Q873536|lt=Sōja}} in {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|en|Okayama Prefecture|WD=Q132936|lt=Okayama Prefecture}}.

Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

Wikidata name: sōja
[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:39, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}}
{{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}

{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole {{ill|Provinces of Japan|en|Provinces of Japan|WD=Q860290|lt=province}}. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara period}} under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>

Whenever a new {{ill|Kokushi (official)|en|Kokushi (official)|WD=Q1351234|lt=kokushi}} was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>

The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}, in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of {{ill|Inaba|en|Inaba|WD=Q79501645|lt=Inaba}}. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>

The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of {{ill|Sōja|en|Sōja|WD=Q873536|lt=Sōja}} in {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|en|Okayama Prefecture|WD=Q132936|lt=Okayama Prefecture}}.

Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

Wikidata name: sōja
[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:39, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}}
{{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}

{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole {{ill|Provinces of Japan|en|Provinces of Japan|WD=Q860290|lt=province}}. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara period}} under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>

Whenever a new {{ill|Kokushi (official)|en|Kokushi (official)|WD=Q1351234|lt=kokushi}} was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>

The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}, in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of {{ill|Inaba|en|Inaba|WD=Q79501645|lt=Inaba}}. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>

The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of {{ill|Sōja|en|Sōja|WD=Q873536|lt=Sōja}} in {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|en|Okayama Prefecture|WD=Q132936|lt=Okayama Prefecture}}.

Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

Wikidata name: sōja
[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:39, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}}
{{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}

{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole {{ill|Provinces of Japan|en|Provinces of Japan|WD=Q860290|lt=province}}. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara period}} under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>

Whenever a new {{ill|Kokushi (official)|en|Kokushi (official)|WD=Q1351234|lt=kokushi}} was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>

The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}, in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of {{ill|Inaba|en|Inaba|WD=Q79501645|lt=Inaba}}. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>

The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of {{ill|Sōja|en|Sōja|WD=Q873536|lt=Sōja}} in {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|en|Okayama Prefecture|WD=Q132936|lt=Okayama Prefecture}}.

Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

Wikidata name: sōja
[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:39, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}}
{{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}

{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole {{ill|Provinces of Japan|en|Provinces of Japan|WD=Q860290|lt=province}}. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara period}} under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>

Whenever a new {{ill|Kokushi (official)|en|Kokushi (official)|WD=Q1351234|lt=kokushi}} was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>

The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}, in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of {{ill|Inaba|en|Inaba|WD=Q79501645|lt=Inaba}}. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>

The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of {{ill|Sōja|en|Sōja|WD=Q873536|lt=Sōja}} in {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|en|Okayama Prefecture|WD=Q132936|lt=Okayama Prefecture}}.

Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

{{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}

{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole {{ill|Provinces of Japan|en|Provinces of Japan|WD=Q860290|lt=province}}. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara period}} under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>

Whenever a new {{ill|Kokushi (official)|en|Kokushi (official)|WD=Q1351234|lt=kokushi}} was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>

The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}, in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of {{ill|Inaba|en|Inaba|WD=Q79501645|lt=Inaba}}. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>

The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of {{ill|Sōja|en|Sōja|WD=Q873536|lt=Sōja}} in {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|en|Okayama Prefecture|WD=Q132936|lt=Okayama Prefecture}}.

Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

{{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}

{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole {{ill|Provinces of Japan|en|Provinces of Japan|WD=Q860290|lt=province}}. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara period}} under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>

Whenever a new {{ill|Kokushi (official)|en|Kokushi (official)|WD=Q1351234|lt=kokushi}} was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>

The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}, in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of {{ill|Inaba|en|Inaba|WD=Q79501645|lt=Inaba}}. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>

The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of {{ill|Sōja|en|Sōja|WD=Q873536|lt=Sōja}} in {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|en|Okayama Prefecture|WD=Q132936|lt=Okayama Prefecture}}.

Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]]

{{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}

{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine|1=Shinto shrine}} where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole {{ill|Provinces of Japan|en|Provinces of Japan|WD=Q860290|lt=province|1=Provinces of Japan}}. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara period|1=Nara period}} under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>

Whenever a new {{ill|Kokushi (official)|en|Kokushi (official)|WD=Q1351234|lt=kokushi|1=Kokushi (official)}} was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>

The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}, in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of {{ill|Inaba|en|Inaba|WD=Q79501645|lt=Inaba|1=Inaba}}. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>

The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of {{ill|Sōja|en|Sōja|WD=Q873536|lt=Sōja|1=Sōja}} in {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|en|Okayama Prefecture|WD=Q132936|lt=Okayama Prefecture|1=Okayama Prefecture}}.

Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

==Regional Soja Shrines==
Regional Soja Shrines are Soja shrines dedicated to a specific region rather than a whole province. These include

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Sōja (Shintō)]][[en:Sōja shrine]][[fr:Sōja (shinto)]][[ja:総社]][[ko:소자 (신토)]][[simple:Sōja shrine]][[zh:總社]]

{{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}

{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine|1=Shinto shrine}} where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole {{ill|Provinces of Japan|en|Provinces of Japan|WD=Q860290|lt=province|1=Provinces of Japan}}. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara period|1=Nara period}} under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>

Whenever a new {{ill|Kokushi (official)|en|Kokushi (official)|WD=Q1351234|lt=kokushi|1=Kokushi (official)}} was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>

The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}, in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of {{ill|Inaba|en|Inaba|WD=Q79501645|lt=Inaba|1=Inaba}}. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>

The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of {{ill|Sōja|en|Sōja|WD=Q873536|lt=Sōja|1=Sōja}} in {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|en|Okayama Prefecture|WD=Q132936|lt=Okayama Prefecture|1=Okayama Prefecture}}.

Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

{{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}

{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine|1=Shinto shrine}} where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole {{ill|Provinces of Japan|en|Provinces of Japan|WD=Q860290|lt=province|1=Provinces of Japan}}. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara period|1=Nara period}} under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>

Whenever a new {{ill|Kokushi (official)|en|Kokushi (official)|WD=Q1351234|lt=kokushi|1=Kokushi (official)}} was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>

The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}, in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of {{ill|Inaba|en|Inaba|WD=Q79501645|lt=Inaba|1=Inaba}}. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>

The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of {{ill|Sōja|en|Sōja|WD=Q873536|lt=Sōja|1=Sōja}} in {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|en|Okayama Prefecture|WD=Q132936|lt=Okayama Prefecture|1=Okayama Prefecture}}.

Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}

{{Other uses|Soja (disambiguation)}}

{{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine|1=Shinto shrine}} where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to as a whole {{ill|Provinces of Japan|en|Provinces of Japan|WD=Q860290|lt=province|1=Provinces of Japan}}. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara period|1=Nara period}} under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.<ref name="Herbert">{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}}</ref>

Whenever a new {{ill|Kokushi (official)|en|Kokushi (official)|WD=Q1351234|lt=kokushi|1=Kokushi (official)}} was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,<ref name="Bocking">{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}}</ref>

The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}, in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of {{ill|Inaba|en|Inaba|WD=Q79501645|lt=Inaba|1=Inaba}}. <ref name="Hardacre">{{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}}</ref>

The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of {{ill|Sōja|en|Sōja|WD=Q873536|lt=Sōja|1=Sōja}} in {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|en|Okayama Prefecture|WD=Q132936|lt=Okayama Prefecture|1=Okayama Prefecture}}.

Rokusho shrine (six place) is a very common Soja shrine name<ref name="Hardacre" />.{{Rp|page=601}}
